aria.name: NSF AI Research Institute on Interaction for AI Assistants (ARIA)
tags: stakeholder participation of people with lived experience
aria.summary: Risk depends on how people come to use and rely on conversational AI over time; recommends trajectory testing, care-connection outcomes, simulation standards, postmarket reassessment, and independent evaluation.
recommendations: Add anticipated patterns of use as a risk factor
Test devices across realistic multi-turn conversations
Require longer premarket studies for heavily used devices
Require evidence that users understand responses, not just disclaimers
Report under- and over-escalation and whether referrals reach care
Track changes in users' help-seeking from people and professionals
Validate synthetic users against data from real users
Report synthetic and real-user results separately
Require a postmarket study when premarket evidence is reduced
Retest against the premarket baseline when the model changes
Require independent evaluation of patient-facing conversational devices
Clarify adverse-event reporting for gradual conversational harms

risk_framework: We propose anticipated patterns of use as a third risk factor, alongside device activity and the consequence of relying on an incorrect or harmful output, to capture how often and how long people use a device and how they rely on it in their decisions and routines.
competency_eval: We support benchmarking followed by clinical confirmation (Q7), with two additions for conversational devices.
synthetic_data: Sponsors should justify the type of synthetic data they use and validate synthetic users against human data (Q13).
third_party: We strongly recommend that the FDA require independent evaluation for all patient-facing conversational devices, especially those people are expected to rely on heavily or use frequently (Q16).
postmarket_tradeoff: The FDA should accept reduced premarket evidence for devices people are expected to use repeatedly or heavily only with a required postmarket study (Q18).
supervisory_agents: Automated monitoring systems should be validated before their results are relied on (Q20).
voluntary_model_files: Voluntary Foundation Model Master Files would support review, but voluntary disclosure alone is not enough.

Where a developer will not disclose safety-relevant information or commit to advance notice of updates, the FDA should require the manufacturer to make up for it through more extensive testing and monitoring.
directiveness_continuum: The FDA should not treat disclaimers as sufficient mitigation when assessing whether a response is action-directing, and should require evidence that intended users understand the device’s responses (Q2).
trajectory_risk: Safety benchmarks should evaluate conversational trajectories (Q5).
escalation_errors: Sponsors of care escalation functions should report both under- and over-escalation and show that referrals work for the intended population (Q3, Q6).
median_clinician_comparator: When clinicians serve as the comparator, sponsors should report performance against both the standard of care and the median clinician the intended population would realistically see, and the FDA should set acceptance criteria against the standard of care for devices people are expected to rely on heavily.
no_care_comparator: The FDA should only allow sponsors to compare a device against delayed care or no care when they show with population-level data, such as coverage, cost, or waitlist data, that this is what intended users would otherwise receive (Q15).
postmarket_methods: Postmarket monitoring should combine user reports with clinician review that protects privacy (Q19).
Re-benchmarking can detect degradation against the capabilities measured before authorization, but it can miss problems that arise when the deployment context changes.

1.title: Question 1
1.quote: Does the two-axis risk framework, organized around device activity and the consequence of relying on an incorrect output, appropriately capture the dimensions most relevant to the risk of a GenAI-enabled software function? If there are additional dimensions—such as the reversibility of a resulting action, the availability of downstream safeguards, the time pressure of the deployment setting, or the traceability of the output (i.e., to primary source materials)—that should be represented in a risk framework, please describe and provide examples of how they should be represented.

2.title: Question 2
2.quote: CDRH seeks input on how to account for the spectrum of GenAI-enabled informational functions that vary in the degree to which they direct a user to a particular action (i.e., between “non-directive” and “action-directing”). What characteristics of an output—such as its wording, specificity, personalization, or context—could be considered as modifiers of the risk associated with an informational function, after accounting for the device’s overall functionality and intended use? What additional information would provide manufacturers with sufficient clarity and predictability around risk assessment for informational functions while recognizing that directiveness may exist along a continuum rather than as a binary distinction?

3.title: Question 3
3.quote: CDRH seeks input on whether and when a GenAI-enabled function that results in delivery of clinical information to patients, as opposed to HCPs, could present different or higher risks, while also recognizing the potential benefits associated with improved patient empowerment, engagement, and access to clinical information. What device characteristics, output features, or safeguards might mitigate risks that could arise when a user lacks the domain knowledge to independently evaluate an output, without unnecessarily underestimating patient capability?

4.title: Question 4
4.quote: CDRH seeks input on whether and how the distinction between generalist and specialist physicians might inform the assessment of risk for HCP-facing GenAI-enabled functions. Under what circumstances, if any, might risk be affected when an HCP who lacks the relevant clinical specialist knowledge receives information that falls within a specialist area of practice? What device characteristics or safeguards might mitigate such risks?

5.title: Question 5
5.quote: For multi-turn conversational GenAI-enabled devices that may migrate from providing “non-directive” information to “action-directing” information over the course of an exchange, how should risk be assessed across realistic conversational trajectories? How could the intended use of such a device be characterized when its behavior is emergent across a conversation?

6.title: Question 6
6.quote: For GenAI-enabled care escalation functions, CDRH is considering how the evaluation may account for both under-escalation and over-escalation. How could manufacturers characterize and weigh these two directions of error, given that they may not be commensurable and that acceptable trade-offs may vary by clinical context?

7.title: Question 7
7.quote: Is the competency-based approach described above, i.e., device benchmarking followed by clinical confirmation, a useful and appropriate framework for evaluating GenAI-enabled devices?

8.title: Question 8
8.quote: How might the two-axis risk framework described in Section IV be considered within the competency-based approach described above to help determine the level of evidence needed for a premarket submission?

9.title: Question 9
9.quote: Would a benchmarking structure such as the one described above be likely to provide adequate evidence of clinical knowledge, analytic capabilities, safety behavior, communication, and generalizability to support a reasonable assurance of safety and effectiveness? Are there elements that are missing, redundant, or inappropriately categorized? Are there externally developed standards that could be leveraged?

10.title: Question 10
10.quote: CDRH recognizes that publicly available benchmarking assets may be subject to data contamination, saturation, and limited real-world representativeness. How should a sponsor establish that performance on a given benchmark predicts safe and effective real-world behavior for the device’s intended use? What evidence should support the construct validity of a benchmark used to gate device evaluation, and what role should sponsor-developed benchmarks play given potential concerns around independence and optimization to the test?

11.title: Question 11
11.quote: CDRH is considering that clinical confirmation for a GenAI-enabled device might not require a prospective clinical study in every case, and has described above a range of approaches of increasing rigor and patient exposure. How might a sponsor select and justify a confirmation approach tailored to a device’s intended use and proportionate to the device’s risk profile? Are there device types or risk profiles for which one or more of these approaches would be insufficient or inappropriate? How might the anticipated distribution of real-world inputs be taken into consideration? Are there other methods of clinical confirmation that might help inform the evaluation of GenAI-enabled devices?

12.title: Question 12
12.quote: How should sponsors achieve statistically meaningful performance measurement for GenAI-enabled devices? Where synthetically generated inputs supplement real patient data, how should sponsors account for differences between the synthetic and real-world distributions when estimating performance, and under what conditions, if any, is it appropriate to combine benchmarking evidence and clinical confirmation evidence to support a single performance estimate?

13.title: Question 13
13.quote: For which clinical domains, device functions, or subpopulations is synthetic data particularly well-suited, or particularly inadequate, as a supplement to real-world evidence? What safeguards would mitigate the risk that synthetic data generated by models of the same class as the device under evaluation reproduces the very performance gaps the evaluation is intended to detect, particularly for underrepresented subgroups?

14.title: Question 14
14.quote: For open-ended device outputs, how should performance comparators and acceptance criteria be selected? When a panel of qualified clinicians serves as the comparator, how should the applicable standard (for example, the standard of care versus the performance of a median clinician in practice) be defined and justified? Should generalist or specialist physicians be used as a performance standard? When should human-AI team performance, rather than the device operating alone, serve as the basis for evaluation?

15.title: Question 15
15.quote: Are there ways in which performance might be assessed relative to the care, technology, or course of action likely to occur in the absence of the device, rather than to the comparators described in this section? What approaches might be used to identify and justify a comparator such as unaided clinical judgment, delayed specialist review, or no intervention?

16.title: Question 16
16.quote: Should independent third parties be involved in some or all aspects of a competency-based approach, including device benchmarking and clinical confirmation? If so, in what ways might qualified, independent third-party participation contribute to this approach, and what qualifications and independence criteria should apply? Are there aspects of the assessment for which third-party involvement would be impractical or inadvisable? What safeguards or program design features would be critical to prevent third-party participation from limiting competition or preventing innovation?

17.title: Question 17
17.quote: CDRH is exploring whether a competency-based approach could be applied to devices that incorporate a variety of underlying model architectures, such as multimodal vision-language models and generative or predictive world models. Are there aspects of the described approach that might be ineffective or inapplicable to these devices? What additional or distinct considerations might need to be addressed?

18.title: Question 18
18.quote: CDRH is considering whether it may be appropriate to accept greater premarket uncertainty regarding a GenAI-enabled device’s benefit-risk profile through greater reliance on postmarket monitoring. Under what conditions might such an approach be appropriate, and what characteristics of a monitoring program would need to be in place to justify reduced premarket evidence? Are there device types or risk profiles for which this approach would not be appropriate?

19.title: Question 19
19.quote: Please comment on the potential approaches to postmarket performance evaluation, including periodic re-benchmarking, sample-based clinician review, and performance degradation monitoring. What additional approaches should CDRH consider, and how should the cadence and triggering events for reassessment be determined?

20.title: Question 20
20.quote: Please comment on whether the proposed approaches to postmarket monitoring can be facilitated by machine-based supervisory agents. What considerations, including the evaluation and reliability of the supervisory agent itself, should CDRH take into account for such an approach?

21.title: Question 21
21.quote: What roles might clinicians, healthcare institutions, professional societies, standards-setting bodies, and other stakeholders appropriately play in postmarket monitoring, and how can these roles be structured without diffusing manufacturer accountability?

22.title: Question 22
22.quote: CDRH envisions that a manufacturer’s premarket competency-based assessment might serve as a baseline against which post-deployment modifications could be re-evaluated. How might the extent of re-benchmarking or other evidence be scaled to the nature and expected impact of a given modification? For example, are there categories of change that might not significantly affect safety or effectiveness of a GenAI-enabled device, or might be appropriately managed within a sponsor’s quality management system versus requiring FDA premarket review and authorization before implementation? Are there categories of changes that might be appropriate for inclusion in a PCCP?

23.title: Question 23
23.quote: How might PCCP concepts or other change-control approaches be adapted for GenAI-enabled devices when the nature or scope of future modifications cannot be fully prespecified?

24.title: Question 24
24.quote: For devices built on third-party foundation models, changes to the underlying model may be initiated by the third-party model developer rather than the device manufacturer. How can a manufacturer detect, evaluate, and respond to such changes in a timely manner? What mechanisms—for example, contractual, technical, or through a PCCP—could provide reasonable assurance that third-party developer-initiated changes do not compromise the safety or effectiveness of the device?

25.title: Question 25
25.quote: Would voluntary Foundation Model MAFs be practical for foundation model developers to provide and to keep current, and what content might they include? Given that participation would be voluntary and that model developers may have limited incentive to disclose safety-relevant information, what would make such a program sufficiently useful for premarket review? Are there alternative mechanisms CDRH should consider for obtaining information about underlying foundation models?

26.title: Question 26
26.quote: Are there additional considerations that inform the premarket and postmarket evaluation of agentic GenAI-enabled devices, beyond those applicable to non-agentic GenAI-enabled devices? How should the elevated risk associated with autonomous multi-step action, tool use, and reduced opportunity for human review be reflected in acceptance criteria and oversight?

IV.title: Section IV, Assessment of Risk
IV.body: Questions 1 to 6. How FDA should rate the risk of a GenAI-enabled function, including what it does on its own, who receives its output, and how risk changes over a conversation.

V.title: Section V, Competency-Based Premarket Evaluation
V.body: Questions 7 to 17. How devices should be tested before reaching the market, including benchmarks, clinical confirmation, synthetic data, comparators, and third-party evaluators.

VI.title: Section VI, Postmarket Monitoring
VI.body: Questions 18 to 24. How devices should be watched and re-evaluated after release, including monitoring, model updates, and change control.

VII.title: Section VII, Other Topics
VII.body: Questions 25 and 26. Information from foundation model developers, and agentic devices that take multi-step actions.

risk_framework.title: Question 1
risk_framework.quote: Does the two-axis risk framework, organized around device activity and the consequence of relying on an incorrect output, appropriately capture the dimensions most relevant to the risk of a GenAI-enabled software function?
risk_framework.body: FDA proposes rating risk on two dimensions. One is how much the device does on its own, from giving information, to directing action, to acting autonomously. The other is how much harm would follow from relying on a wrong output.

directiveness_continuum.title: Question 2
directiveness_continuum.quote: What additional information would provide manufacturers with sufficient clarity and predictability around risk assessment for informational functions while recognizing that directiveness may exist along a continuum rather than as a binary distinction?
directiveness_continuum.body: FDA suggests that how strongly an output steers a user toward an action is a matter of degree, and that features such as wording, specificity, and personalization could raise or lower the risk of an informational function.

patient_facing_risk.title: Question 3
patient_facing_risk.quote: CDRH seeks input on whether and when a GenAI-enabled function that results in delivery of clinical information to patients, as opposed to HCPs, could present different or higher risks, while also recognizing the potential benefits associated with improved patient empowerment, engagement, and access to clinical information.
patient_facing_risk.body: Whether a device that gives clinical information directly to patients, who may not be able to judge whether it is right, should be treated as riskier than one used by clinicians, and what safeguards would help without underestimating patients.

trajectory_risk.title: Question 5
trajectory_risk.quote: For multi-turn conversational GenAI-enabled devices that may migrate from providing “non-directive” information to “action-directing” information over the course of an exchange, how should risk be assessed across realistic conversational trajectories?
trajectory_risk.body: Judging a conversational device by how whole conversations unfold, since a chat that starts with general information can drift toward telling the user what to do, instead of judging each response on its own.

escalation_errors.title: Question 6
escalation_errors.quote: For GenAI-enabled care escalation functions, CDRH is considering how the evaluation may account for both under-escalation and over-escalation.
escalation_errors.body: For devices that decide when to send a user to a clinician or emergency care, measuring both failures to escalate when needed and escalations that were not needed, and weighing the two by clinical context.

competency_eval.title: Question 7
competency_eval.quote: Is the competency-based approach described above, i.e., device benchmarking followed by clinical confirmation, a useful and appropriate framework for evaluating GenAI-enabled devices?
competency_eval.body: Modeled loosely on how physicians are trained and examined. A device would first be scored on benchmarks of clinical knowledge, safety behavior, communication, and generalizability, then its performance would be confirmed in clinical use as actually configured.

confirmation_flex.title: Question 11
confirmation_flex.quote: CDRH is considering that clinical confirmation for a GenAI-enabled device might not require a prospective clinical study in every case, and has described above a range of approaches of increasing rigor and patient exposure.
confirmation_flex.body: FDA suggests that lower-risk devices could confirm performance with lighter methods, such as retrospective review, running silently alongside clinicians, or clinician adjudication, before or instead of a new prospective study.

synthetic_data.title: Question 12
synthetic_data.quote: Where synthetically generated inputs supplement real patient data, how should sponsors account for differences between the synthetic and real-world distributions when estimating performance
synthetic_data.body: Using computer-generated test cases or simulated patients alongside real patient data when evaluating a device.

median_clinician_comparator.title: Question 14
median_clinician_comparator.quote: When a panel of qualified clinicians serves as the comparator, how should the applicable standard (for example, the standard of care versus the performance of a median clinician in practice) be defined and justified?
median_clinician_comparator.body: Whether a device should be compared with what a typical clinician actually does in practice, or only with the standard of care.

no_care_comparator.title: Question 15
no_care_comparator.quote: Are there ways in which performance might be assessed relative to the care, technology, or course of action likely to occur in the absence of the device, rather than to the comparators described in this section?
no_care_comparator.body: Comparing a device with what patients would likely get without it, such as unaided judgment, a long wait for a specialist, or no care at all, instead of with clinicians.

third_party.title: Question 16
third_party.quote: Should independent third parties be involved in some or all aspects of a competency-based approach, including device benchmarking and clinical confirmation?
third_party.body: Having organizations independent of the manufacturer run or check some of the benchmarking or clinical confirmation, instead of relying only on the manufacturer's own testing.

postmarket_tradeoff.title: Question 18
postmarket_tradeoff.quote: CDRH is considering whether it may be appropriate to accept greater premarket uncertainty regarding a GenAI-enabled device’s benefit-risk profile through greater reliance on postmarket monitoring.
postmarket_tradeoff.body: Letting a device reach the market with less evidence up front, in exchange for closer monitoring after release.

postmarket_methods.title: Question 19
postmarket_methods.quote: Please comment on the potential approaches to postmarket performance evaluation, including periodic re-benchmarking, sample-based clinician review, and performance degradation monitoring.
postmarket_methods.body: FDA's proposed ways of checking a device after release: rerunning benchmarks periodically, having clinicians review a sample of outputs, and watching for declines in performance.

supervisory_agents.title: Question 20
supervisory_agents.quote: Please comment on whether the proposed approaches to postmarket monitoring can be facilitated by machine-based supervisory agents.
supervisory_agents.body: Using AI systems to monitor a deployed device's outputs after release, for example flagging errors or drift for human review.

flexible_change_control.title: Question 23
flexible_change_control.quote: How might PCCP concepts or other change-control approaches be adapted for GenAI-enabled devices when the nature or scope of future modifications cannot be fully prespecified?
flexible_change_control.body: A predetermined change control plan (PCCP) lets a manufacturer get approval in advance for planned updates, so they don't each need new FDA review. FDA asks how this could cover updates to generative models that can't be fully spelled out ahead of time.

voluntary_model_files.title: Question 25
voluntary_model_files.quote: Would voluntary Foundation Model MAFs be practical for foundation model developers to provide and to keep current, and what content might they include?
voluntary_model_files.body: Companies that build the underlying AI models could voluntarily give FDA confidential information about their models in a master file (MAF), which device makers could then reference.

agentic_oversight.title: Question 26
agentic_oversight.quote: How should the elevated risk associated with autonomous multi-step action, tool use, and reduced opportunity for human review be reflected in acceptance criteria and oversight?
agentic_oversight.body: Whether devices that act on their own across several steps, use other software tools, or leave less room for human review should face stricter acceptance criteria and oversight than other generative AI devices.

Reliance, sycophancy, and affective harm.body: Users coming to depend on AI, AI telling users what they want to hear, and emotional harms.

Hallucination and output reliability.body: Made-up or inconsistent output, and outputs that drift or change between runs.

Runtime controls and kill switches.body: Controls that limit or stop a device while it runs, such as permission checks, hard limits, and off switches.

Audit trails, provenance, and records.body: Records that show what a device did, with which model version, and based on what sources.

Cybersecurity.body: Attacks on devices, including prompt injection, and the integrity of their inputs.

Privacy and consent.body: Protecting patient data, limits on its use, and patient consent.

Liability and accountability.body: Who is legally responsible when AI contributes to harm, and how accountability is enforced.

Equity, access, and disability.body: Performance across populations, access to care, and users with disabilities.

Human oversight and automation bias.body: Whether human review works in practice, including clinicians over-trusting AI and clinician workload.

Small developer burden.body: Costs and requirements that fall hardest on small companies.

Coverage and reimbursement.body: Insurance coverage and payment for AI-enabled care.

Deployment settings and infrastructure.body: Where and how devices run, such as hospitals, homes, offline settings, and local validation.

Transparency and public participation.body: Disclosure to patients and the public, labeling, and involving stakeholders in oversight.

Regulatory process and harmonization.body: Regulatory pathways, standards, terminology, and coordination with other agencies and countries.

Opposition to AI use.body: Objections to using generative AI in health care at all.

Other.body: Specialty-specific or one-off topics that fit no other theme.

support.body: Endorses the proposal as described, or with minor tweaks.

conditional.body: Supports the proposal only with substantial conditions, limits, or safeguards the comment treats as necessary.

oppose.body: Argues against the proposal, says it is insufficient or inappropriate, or calls for a materially different approach.

median_clinician_comparator.reason: Comparisons should use safe, adequately staffed care, not understaffed practice
median_clinician_comparator.alternative: Compare against safe, adequately staffed care

voluntary_model_files.reason: Developers have strong competitive incentives to withhold information, so voluntary files will not work
voluntary_model_files.alternative: Higher premarket evidence burden for devices lacking a complete master file

voluntary_model_files.reason: Hosted models change every few minutes, so no master file can stay current
voluntary_model_files.alternative: User-side records of which model answered and device-held lineage records

voluntary_model_files.reason: Model developers have limited commercial incentive to disclose safety-relevant limitations of their models
voluntary_model_files.alternative: Mandatory foundation model disclosure for higher-consequence devices

voluntary_model_files.reason: Foundation model developers have no incentive to participate in a voluntary program
voluntary_model_files.alternative: Mandatory foundation model disclosure for any model in regulated devices

voluntary_model_files.reason: Voluntary files draw disclosure only from developers with little to hide
voluntary_model_files.alternative: Mandatory developer documentation or the sponsor carries the full evidence burden

patient_facing_risk.reason: Risk depends on the user's verification path, not on whether the user is a patient
patient_facing_risk.alternative: Assess risk by the availability and latency of the user's verification path

patient_facing_risk.reason: Patient-facing use should not by itself create a presumption of higher risk
patient_facing_risk.alternative: Treat user comprehension and adaptive communication as potential risk controls

patient_facing_risk.reason: Patient-facing should not be a per se risk elevation when the alternative is unvetted internet content
patient_facing_risk.alternative: Credit verifiable behaviors like non-directive frames and forced deferral

patient_facing_risk.reason: Credentials are a poor proxy for the ability to evaluate outputs, and patients can be expert
patient_facing_risk.alternative: Device-specific competency affirmation scaled to risk instead of user categories

patient_facing_risk.reason: Patient-facing AI is not automatically higher risk and should not be penalized by default
patient_facing_risk.alternative: Scale burden to clinical consequence with patient-specific safeguards

patient_facing_risk.reason: User status is a poor proxy for risk compared with reviewability and verification time
patient_facing_risk.alternative: Assess reviewability, certainty, verification time, and capacity for action

directiveness_continuum.reason: Directive outputs amount to medical advice, so all outputs need required informational modifiers
directiveness_continuum.alternative: Require linguistic modifiers marking unapproved outputs as for information only

directiveness_continuum.reason: Wording and tone are hard to define and manufacturers can change wording without changing function
directiveness_continuum.alternative: One division between general and patient-specific output, then classify by consequence

directiveness_continuum.reason: Directiveness varied with user affect rather than with the function or its intended use
directiveness_continuum.alternative: Assign the highest risk class reachable on a trajectory and test varying affect

directiveness_continuum.reason: An axis based on output wording can be moved by rewording without changing user options
directiveness_continuum.alternative: Define the axis by the function's effect on the user's choice set

directiveness_continuum.reason: Risk should follow what an output asserts, not how directive it sounds
directiveness_continuum.alternative: Grade outputs by significance, whether they present or generate claims

third_party.reason: A third-party requirement invites organizations to game the system and profit from prolonged testing
Requiring independent benchmarks would leave small developers in novel domains with no benchmark
third_party.alternative: Full public disclosure of sponsor-developed benchmarks, rubrics, and outputs

risk_framework.reason: Device activity does not equal probability of harm, so the two axes are insufficient
risk_framework.alternative: Standard probability and severity risk analysis with modifiers like reversibility

escalation_errors.reason: For protocol delivery, escalation is a protocol step, not a trade-off between two error rates
escalation_errors.alternative: Evaluate escalation ordering per scenario as a protocol fidelity item

postmarket_tradeoff.reason: Postmarket monitoring should verify premarket claims, not substitute for inadequate premarket evidence
postmarket_tradeoff.alternative: Risk-tiered premarket evidence, with prospective clinical studies for high-risk devices

postmarket_tradeoff.reason: Postmarket review is not enough for a new technology with many unknowns
postmarket_tradeoff.alternative: Require manufacturers to prove minimum accuracy before approval

postmarket_tradeoff.reason: Accepting premarket uncertainty shifts risk to patients, and postmarket surveillance cannot detect GenAI failures
postmarket_tradeoff.alternative: Limit relief to the lowest-risk quadrant with GenAI-specific reporting safeguards

postmarket_tradeoff.reason: Postmarket monitoring must supplement strong premarket evidence so patients are not test subjects
postmarket_tradeoff.alternative: Strong premarket evidence supplemented by postmarket monitoring

postmarket_tradeoff.reason: Reduced premarket evidence moves discovery of uncertainty onto patients through harm
postmarket_tradeoff.alternative: Postmarket monitoring as a complement to premarket evidence

flexible_change_control.reason: A PCCP cannot cover foundation model changes the sponsor does not control
flexible_change_control.alternative: Version pinning, change notification, no silent updates, and re-benchmarking

flexible_change_control.reason: Material model changes should be caught before affecting care and get revalidation and FDA review
flexible_change_control.alternative: Version traceability, revalidation, FDA review, suspension and rollback controls

no_care_comparator.reason: Weak real-world care as a comparator can make a product appear beneficial
no_care_comparator.alternative: Compare against safe, adequately staffed care

no_care_comparator.reason: An unavailable alternative changes a device's benefit, not the consequence of its errors
no_care_comparator.alternative: Absolute prespecified thresholds informed by specialist standard of care

confirmation_flex.reason: Benchmarks cannot capture real human interaction, so prospective studies should establish safety
confirmation_flex.alternative: Prospective clinical studies for devices that directly influence patient care

competency_eval.reason: Open-endedness is a design choice, so bounded devices should use established methods
competency_eval.alternative: Make bounding the primary expectation and justify competency evaluation otherwise

nopos.point: Medical AI may carry demographic and subjective bias and erode patient agency and personhood
Generative AI in health care is too risky now because of hallucinations and privacy
Devices should not be used until bias, privacy, and legal liability questions are settled
Internet connectivity is an issue for some families
Product liability law already holds AI makers accountable, so markets rather than regulators should constrain AI
Devices should be cleared only after formal requirements, specifications, verification, and definitive validation
Rural hospitals need receiving facilities and insurers to accept AI stroke CT reads for transfers
Personal grievance about alleged fraud, paternity orders, and loss of control over identity and records
Patients must consent to voice print use in AI training because voice prints cannot be deidentified
Test whether devices recognize when medical evidence is weak, using historical medical reversals as benchmarks
Audit how clinician responses to AI outputs are used, and record reasons when dismissed
Medical AI should impartially weigh global evidence, including complementary and traditional medicine, by equal standards
Clarify what counts as generative AI and consider a parallel proposal for causal AI
Treat where the output appears in the clinician workflow as part of the device being evaluated
Clarify the boundary between AI that conveys a clinician's plan and AI exercising independent judgment
Attachment reproduces FDA's discussion paper with no added commentary
Involve patients, clinicians, and many other stakeholders in oversight throughout the AI lifecycle
Require standardized, machine checkable documentation and versioning of datasets used in device evaluation
Manage silent third party model updates through local model locking and automated drift detection
Assess whether evaluation and monitoring layers provide truly independent evidence about device failure

open_questions.question: Should patient-facing use raise a device's risk level?

sides.label: Yes, in some cases or with safeguards
No, risk depends on whether users can check the output

open_questions.question: What should a device's performance be compared against?

sides.label: The standard of care, not a typical clinician
What patients would get without the device

open_questions.question: Can voluntary disclosure from model developers give FDA what it needs?

sides.label: Yes, if the device maker stays responsible for safety
No, disclosure should be required or the evidence burden raised

open_questions.question: How far can postmarket monitoring stand in for premarket evidence?

sides.label: Only if monitoring is shown to catch failures before harm

open_questions.question: Should directiveness be judged by an output's wording or by its effect?

sides.label: By degree, including wording, specificity, and context
By what the output claims or does, since wording is easy to change

recs.label: Add reversibility, detectability, and traceability to risk ratings
recs.desc: Expand the two-axis risk framework with factors such as reversibility, time to harm, error detectability, human review, and traceability to source evidence.

recs.label: Judge directiveness by behavior and discount disclaimers
recs.desc: Classify how directive a device is from what its outputs do, with rubrics or worked examples, and give no risk credit for disclaimers or labels alone.

recs.label: Ease rules for clinician supervised and informational tools
recs.desc: Place clinician-supervised or purely informational functions in lower risk tiers, streamlined pathways, or enforcement discretion.

recs.label: Publish a map from risk tier to required evidence
recs.desc: Publish guidance linking each risk position to the minimum evidence and clinical confirmation expected.

recs.label: Test devices across long conversations and repeated sessions
recs.desc: Evaluate behavior over whole conversations, late turns, repeated sessions, and stored user state instead of single prompts.

recs.label: Test whether outputs shift under user pressure
recs.desc: Benchmark whether advice changes with user affect, displeasure, reassurance, claimed authority, or beliefs when the clinical facts stay the same.

recs.label: Test for made up output when input is missing
recs.desc: Check that devices do not produce confident output when sensor, image, or other input is missing, broken, or null, and log such cases.

recs.label: Report under and over escalation separately
recs.desc: Report missed and unnecessary escalations as separate rates with prespecified, justified tolerances.

recs.label: Set separate pass or fail limits for critical failures
recs.desc: Set non-averageable thresholds for named high-consequence failures that a device must meet regardless of overall scores.

recs.label: Enforce safety rules outside the generative model
recs.desc: Use deterministic architecture and controls outside the model, and avoid relying on prompts, for scope limits and safety behaviors.

recs.label: Test for prompt injection, security, and dependency failures
recs.desc: Test resistance to prompt injection and cyber threats and verify safe behavior when connectivity, suppliers, or dependencies fail.

recs.label: Show benchmarks and reference ratings are valid and reliable
recs.desc: Require evidence that benchmarks measure what they claim, results reproduce across runs, datasets are documented, and human reference panels are qualified and agree.

recs.label: Use sequestered shared benchmarks and check contamination
recs.desc: Hold out sequestered or shared standard test sets, including ones qualified through FDA programs, and check for training-data contamination.

recs.label: Keep synthetic and real data results separate
recs.desc: Report synthetic and real-world results separately, validate synthetic data against real data, and do not let synthetic data alone set performance rates.

recs.label: Compare devices against realistic standards of care
recs.desc: Choose comparators that reflect the realistic alternative a patient would face, such as standard of care or no device, instead of a median clinician default.

recs.label: Evaluate clinicians and AI together as deployed
recs.desc: Measure performance of the human and device working together in the real workflow, alongside device-alone results.

recs.label: Show that human oversight works in practice
recs.desc: Credit human review only when testing shows users catch and override errors, including human factors and automation bias testing.

recs.label: Evaluate the full deployed system including prompts
recs.desc: Treat the exact deployed configuration, including prompts, retrieval, tools, and orchestration, as the thing tested and controlled.

recs.label: Test across populations, settings, and atypical cases
recs.desc: Evaluate performance across subgroups, children, rural and low-resource settings, and hard or out-of-distribution cases.

recs.label: Require prospective outcome studies for high risk devices
recs.desc: Require prospective clinical studies measuring patient outcomes or clinical utility for high-risk or action-directing devices.

recs.label: Restrict trading premarket evidence for postmarket monitoring
recs.desc: Allow reduced premarket evidence only for low-risk functions where failures are detectable and reversible and monitoring is in place.

recs.label: Prespecify postmarket triggers, thresholds, and responses
recs.desc: Make postmarket monitoring plans enforceable with set metrics, thresholds, cadence, event triggers, and corrective actions.

recs.label: Monitor for drift and unannounced model changes
recs.desc: Detect performance drift and silent upstream model changes after launch with canary tests, golden suites, or output monitoring.

recs.label: Monitor with records the device cannot alter
recs.desc: Base monitoring and evidence on independent records outside the device's control instead of the device's own self-reports.

recs.label: Retest against the baseline whenever the model changes
recs.desc: Re-run benchmarks against the premarket baseline before deploying any model, prompt, or configuration change.

recs.label: Pin model versions and require notice of changes
recs.desc: Lock foundation model versions, forbid silent updates, and require advance notice of supplier model changes.

recs.label: Limit preapproved change plans to bounded changes
recs.desc: Define predetermined change control plans as bounded envelopes or categories of change with set verification and rollback.

recs.label: Require model developers to share model information
recs.desc: Require foundation model developers to disclose model information through master files, contracts, or model cards, with manufacturers characterizing models otherwise.

recs.label: Keep accountability clear and centered on manufacturers
recs.desc: Keep manufacturers responsible for model validity and monitoring despite master files or deployers, and assign clear legal accountability for harms.

recs.label: Keep tamper evident records including model version
recs.desc: Keep tamper-evident logs that can reconstruct events, including the model version, configuration, and human decisions behind each output.

recs.label: Require human approval before consequential or irreversible actions
recs.desc: Require a qualified human to approve consequential clinical decisions and irreversible agentic actions before they happen.

recs.label: Define and enforce limits on agent authority
recs.desc: Specify what agentic devices may access and do, enforce least privilege, and check permissions at the time of each action.

recs.label: Test agents across the full sequence of actions
recs.desc: Evaluate agentic systems on their whole action trajectory, including retries and delegation, beyond final endpoints.

recs.label: Validate supervisory AI agents and keep human review
recs.desc: Validate AI monitors independently of the device they supervise, using different models, and keep them below human review.

recs.label: Require a tested off switch and rollback
recs.desc: Require tested ways to stop, suspend, or roll back a device or agent quickly.

recs.label: Tell patients when AI shapes their care
recs.desc: Disclose to patients, and seek consent where needed, when AI substantially participates in their care.

recs.label: Protect patient data and limit secondary use
recs.desc: Protect patient data, treat data sensitivity as a risk factor, and limit collection, retention, and secondary uses such as training.

recs.label: Clarify and expand reporting of AI errors and harms
recs.desc: Clarify adverse event reporting for generative errors and gradual harms and give patients and clinicians channels to report problems.

recs.label: Require independent third party evaluation
recs.desc: Require or accredit independent evaluators, free of conflicts, to test devices instead of relying only on sponsor testing.

recs.label: Align terms and standards across agencies and countries
recs.desc: Use consistent AI terminology across FDA and other agencies and harmonize with international and existing standards.

method: 124 posted comments read in full, including attachments, and coded against the codebook. A question counts as addressed when a comment discusses it substantively, cited or not. Comment types come from Regulations.gov; those with no category were assigned from content and are marked inferred.
